text:
Summary

Guidance from the Department for Education (DfE) and the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) on the safe, responsible and appropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI) in children’s and adult social care in England.

It is intended to help local authorities, social care organisations and practitioners consider how AI may be used responsibly in practice.

It is not a technical guide and does not replace existing legal, regulatory or professional requirements.

DfE and DHSC recognise that, used appropriately, AI can support children’s and adult social care.

AI has the potential to:

support better outcomes

create more time for meaningful engagement with individuals and families

help practitioners develop a more informed and reflective understanding

identify gaps in information and help organisations make better use of information

support resource planning

strengthen decision-making and strategic oversight

Social care is fundamentally relationship-based. AI should always strengthen, not replace, human connection, professional judgement and accountability.

AI use raises ethical questions around:

accuracy and bias

transparency

consent

accountability

data protection

security risks

Local authorities and social care organisations should ensure AI use is governed appropriately. There should be clear guardrails in place, including:

acceptable use

data handling rules

training and supervision

monitoring and review

Responsibility and accountability remain with practitioners and their organisations.

Organisations should provide clarity on the AI tools that can be used to support practice, and the parameters that govern this use. No personal data should be entered into publicly available AI tools operating outside the organisation’s secure environment or enterprise agreements that protect onward sharing or use of data.

Decisions about whether or how to adopt AI remain with organisations and should be taken in line with their:

legal duties

local policies

data protection arrangements

professional standards and responsibilities

This guidance is intended to provide a foundation for DfE and DHSC to develop further resources (jointly where appropriate) to support ongoing responsible implementation, use and governance of AI tools in social care.

Who this publication is for

This guidance highlights universal themes applicable across organisations within children’s and adult social care. We understand that approaches will vary across local areas and organisations. The application of the guidance is at the discretion of the organisation.

This guidance is for:

frontline practitioners

supervisors

managers

digital and data teams

transformation teams

data protection officers

Caldicott guardians

procurement staff

other organisations providing social care and related services

The principles of this guidance will also apply to other organisations providing social care and related services.

Using this guidance

This guidance is intended to set out DfE and DHSC’s position on AI in social care and provide high-level guidance on its opportunities, risks and ethics.

We would recommend that the whole document is read and understood, but the following sections may help with specific queries:

how AI may support children’s and adult social care may help transformation or technical staff identify where AI could support practice

considerations for organisations and practitioners may be useful for practitioners and supervisors in understanding how to safely use AI in practice

considerations for the appropriate use of AI may also help managers and technical or transformation staff create the guardrails to support the safe use of AI

ethics, risks and challenges may help practitioners and supervisors understand the different risks and ethical dilemmas they may encounter when using AI

Using AI in social care: a quick guide for practitioners may help those new or unfamiliar with AI understand the basics

DfE has guidance on Generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education.

Main points

AI in this document means the tools used to:

generate, summarise, transcribe or organise information

support service improvement, communication, accessibility and analysis in support of children’s and adult social care practice

AI, used responsibly, can support social care practice by:

strengthening relationship-based and reflective practice

improving how information is used

testing assumptions

identifying gaps and reducing administrative burdens

strengthening services and supporting better decisions

AI is not infallible – it makes mistakes and practitioners should challenge AI outputs.

Responsibility and accountability remain with practitioners and their organisations. AI outputs should be treated as a first draft to be reviewed and amended before use.

Risks including bias, inaccuracy or hallucinations, privacy and security concerns, and automation bias (where AI outputs may be given undue weight by practitioners) should be identified and managed.

Practitioners should be able to clearly explain the AI tools being used, why, and what will be done with the outputs. This helps build trust and transparency.

Local authorities and social care organisations should have or be working to implement governance (including AI use policies), assurance and practical guardrails so AI is used safely, lawfully and appropriately.

Only platforms that are secure and data protection compliant should be used, and in line with organisational policies. Personal data should not be entered into AI tools that have not been approved by the organisation, as these are not secure.

The use of AI in social care should not jeopardise or impede the relational values of care, individual rights and dignities.

AI is not sentient and does not understand the personal contexts of a child, family, individual or their lived experiences. AI should not replace practitioners’ judgement or make automated decisions about risk, need, eligibility or intervention.

DfE and DHSC’s position: 4 principles for the use of AI in social care

This guidance is non-statutory and should be applied in line with local policies, governance arrangements and professional standards. DfE’s and DHSC’s view is that:

1. Practitioners remain responsible for their casework, recording and decision-making. AI-generated content should be treated as a first draft and reviewed, challenged and amended where necessary to ensure it reflects context, observations and critical reflections.

2. AI should not make decisions that directly affect people. Decisions relating to risk, need, eligibility, safeguarding, care planning and intervention should remain the responsibility of practitioners exercising professional judgement.

3. AI should support better experiences and outcomes for children, adults and families. It should strengthen relationship-based practice by improving communications, reducing the burden of administrative tasks, supporting access to information and helping practitioners spend more time working directly with people.

4. Personal information should not be entered into publicly accessible AI tools. AI should only be used in line with organisational policies, using approved tools and according to data protection policies.

AI is not sentient and does not understand the personal contexts of a child, family or individual or their lived experiences. AI should not replace practitioners’ judgement or make automated decisions about risk, need, eligibility or intervention.

AI and human relationships

Social care is relationship-based, and AI has the potential to influence human connection both positively and negatively. It may support practitioners to reduce administrative tasks and reflect on their practice, but if implemented poorly it may reduce opportunities for meaningful engagement and undermine trust.

Responsible and appropriate use of AI should consider how AI supports the values of care and does not erode them. The adoption of AI in social care should not be judged solely by efficiency gains but also by how it contributes to better experiences and stronger human connections.

Organisations and practitioners should be aware of the impact that the increasing focus on the use of AI (and other digital tools) may have on those experiencing digital exclusion. Some children, families, carers or individuals drawing on care and support may:

have low levels of digital confidence

have limited access to devices or connectivity

require support to engage with technology

experience cognitive impairments that affect digital participation

Taking an ethically robust, transparent and well-governed approach to implementing AI, built around the relationships and importance of human connection may help mitigate against the use of AI widening the digital exclusion divide.

Organisations developing tools or shaping implementation may want to consider how young people, families or individuals drawing on care can be involved in service design or governance. This can help mitigate against other forms of potential digital exclusion such as literacy barriers, under-representation and inaccessible outputs.

How AI may support children’s and adult social care

Social care has a significant impact on the lives of the individuals and families supported by practitioners. Children, families or individuals drawing on care should be at the heart of every decision made about them.

AI should support practitioners and relationship-based, person-centred care – not replace their professional judgement.

Support and reduce administrative burden

AI tools have the potential to reduce the time spent on routine and repetitive tasks, particularly recording and paperwork, although their effectiveness and safety can vary. For example, AI tools may be able to:

support speech‑to‑text transcription of visits, meetings and supervision notes, with practitioners reviewing, ensuring factors such as body language, physical environment, tone of voice and other areas not picked up by AI are reflected

help draft case notes, reports, chronologies and letters, which practitioners review, amend and finalise

structure and format records in line with agreed templates and recording standards, with practitioners checking for accuracy and bias

help ensure children, families and carers, and those who draw on care are heard and their voice and needs are accurately reflected in their care notes

Case study: Kingston Council

A local authority introduced an AI-enabled tool to support them to draft case notes, assessments and supervision records in adult social care. The initiative was driven by increasing demand for services and a desire to reduce the amount of time practitioners spent on administrative tasks. This would allow them to focus more time on direct work with people who draw on care and support.

The tool helped practitioners transcribe and summarise conversations into draft records, which remained subject to practitioner review and approval. Social workers reported an average of 50 to 60 per cent reduction in time spent completing case notes and assessments. Supervision write-ups reduced from 40 minutes to less than 10 minutes.

Kingston Council: Using AI in Adult Social Care administration Local Government Association has more information.

AI tools, used effectively, also have the potential to support improvements to workforce wellbeing by reducing frustration linked to high workloads and heavy recording requirements, which can contribute to stress and burnout.

Case study: Together for Children Sunderland

When evaluating the impact of AI during the implementation of an AI-enabled transcription tool, Together for Children Sunderland worked with social workers to understand the impact on workforce wellbeing.

The evaluation involved:

journey mapping practitioners’ day-to-day experiences before and after adopting AI

baseline data collection

time-motion studies

practitioner feedback

post-pilot surveys

The results found:

reductions in the time spent on administrative tasks

improvements to worker wellbeing and mental health

reductions in stress

productivity benefits

improved quality of conversations and case recordings

Improving the quality and consistency of case recording and care planning

AI tools may support higher quality case records and care planning by:

reducing unnecessary repetition across assessments, plans and meeting records

supporting clearer and more concise writing, while allowing practitioners to apply their professional judgement and narrative

supporting the removal of judgemental or victim-blaming language that can be re-traumatising to individuals reviewing their records

helping improve the quality of writing and use of appropriate language for example:

using ‘language that cares’ and writing ‘to’ individuals

identifying bias, subjectivity and errors

identifying areas where additional information or reflection may be needed, such as analysis, next steps and the voice of the individual in records

offering the potential to pre-fill data fields in case-records

helping staff to better use information in their professional judgement

This can support better-informed decision-making by helping practitioners:

identify relevant information

understand patterns across complex case records

highlight gaps for further enquiry

access evidence more efficiently

The final decision should always remain with the practitioner.

Supporting good practice

AI tools may be able to support relational and strengths-based practice by:

allowing practitioners to be more focused on direct work and engagement with people who draw on care, children, families and carers

supporting practitioners to prepare for visits, interactions and conversations

supporting practitioners’ professional curiosity and thinking by structuring information, testing analysis, identifying gaps, and challenging assumptions

helping practitioners test analysis and challenge assumptions

Case study: Norfolk County Council fostering teams

Norfolk County Council’s fostering team used a Microsoft Copilot custom-built supervision agent. This was embedded with National Minimum Standards, relevant legislation and local guidance to support reflective drafting and structured analysis.

The agent analyses transcripts alongside the supervising social worker’s notes, observations and reflections to produce a structured first draft of a supervision record.

This supports deeper reflection, sharper analysis and clearer professional judgement, reinforcing rather than replacing professional expertise. This has led to clear, more consistent and more analytically rigorous supervision records.

Supporting the use of information in cases, case records and care planning

AI may help practitioners find and use information more easily, especially in long or complex case records. For example, AI enabled tools have the potential to:

help staff quickly understand and search case histories to find relevant information;

produce summaries of lengthy records to support preparation for visits and reviews

highlight missing sections or gaps that may need further consideration

retrieve and summarise information from multiple systems

This can support better‑informed decision‑making, while decisions remain with practitioners.

Supporting reflection, supervision and workforce wellbeing

AI’s ability to process and summarise complex information has the potential to enhance practitioner reflection and supervision. This includes:

helping practitioners prepare reflective summaries for supervision, for example through posing reflective questions, or prompting curiosity

supporting supervisors to identify themes across workloads, while maintaining accountability for decisions

Supporting reasonable adjustments

AI may help local authorities support practitioners, children, parents and carers and people who draw on care and support, by removing disability-related barriers to:

communication

comprehension

drafting

information processing

This can support:

the creation of accessible versions of information for children, young people and adults with different communication needs

reasonable adjustments for practitioners, making the career more accessible

Supporting integration

AI has the potential to support integration between systems, both within organisations and across organisational boundaries. This may include improving the sharing of information between practitioners and other agencies, extending beyond individual interactions with social care services. This will help to deliver more integrated care across the wider health and care ecosystem.

For this to be effective, tools will need to be tested for accuracy and security, grounded in relevant materials, and subject to effective governance. Where information or systems span organisational boundaries, appropriate agreements will also need to be in place.

Strategic analysis, commissioning and planning

AI’s ability to process and analyse large datasets may help organisations develop strategic insights to support planning, resource management and strategic decision-making.

AI may also help organisations identify gaps in provision and highlight emerging pressures or risks that may require further consideration. This can support more informed planning and decision making across the social care system.

For example, AI used in this capacity may help organisations:

analyse demand, referral patterns, waiting times or identify changes in demand for services

identify gaps in local support and provisions or unmet needs

help leaders understand workforce pressures and service bottlenecks

identify emerging pressures and risks on service provision

identify commissioning needs and support procurement decisions

evaluate the impact of services

support earlier planning for placement sufficiency, care packages or community support

Exploring AI’s capability to analyse large amounts of data could also support better strategic commissioning through the development of more accurate, data-driven and evidence-led needs assessments and forecasts.

There is limited evidence of the use of this aspect of AI across social care, there are examples of local authorities using this capability to support other areas, such as housing and waste.

Case study: AI in Swindon Borough Council’s Adult Social Care

Swindon piloted an AI tool to support social workers. They recognised the impact that administrative tasks have on the time available for social workers to focus on person-centred care. This can be amplified for colleagues with learning difficulties or other protected characteristics.

The pilot found:

a 63% reduction in admin time, helping them to allocate more time to supporting individuals

faster assessments – the time to conduct a Care Act Conversation fell from 1.5 hours to 30 minutes, and time taken to write up assessments fell from 4 hours to 1.5 hours

The tool has been particularly beneficial for colleagues with learning difficulties, visual impairments, and those where English is not their first language. Dyslexic social workers and those with learning difficulties reported benefits in their practice and recording.

More information is available from the news article: Council completes AI trial to enhance Adult Social Care services Swindon Borough Council.

Translation

AI-enabled translation may support practitioners to undertake direct work with families where English is not their first, or spoken, language. This may reduce barriers and improve timeliness where there could be delays in finding a translator.

Case study: using AI to improve accessibility

A significant proportion of care leavers, particularly unaccompanied asylum-seeking children (UASC), have English as a second language or speak no English at all. Approximately 25% of care leavers cannot access the digital information and support provided. Research found many care leavers were unaware of the support available when leaving care.

AI Solution

The Support for Care Leavers website uses AI-powered translation to provide content in more than 100 languages. The tool generates translations instantly, allowing users to access information in their preferred language without requiring manual translation.

Outcome

AI has enabled a more accessible and inclusive service, helping more care leavers understand their rights and the support available as they transition to independent living.

Implications

AI-powered translation can enhance digital accessibility and, where integrated with wider services, help people to find the right support earlier. It can also help to facilitate informed decision-making, reduce pressure on services and can improve outcomes for councils and communities across children’s and adult social care.

Where AI-enabled translation tools are being used, organisations should ensure processes are in place to ensure and evaluate accuracy – particularly where translations are likely to be used in a statutory process. In these cases, organisations should consider when a qualified interpreter is required, rather than relying solely on AI-enabled translation.

Translation tools are also supporting social workers who have English as a second language to check and improve their written English. This may carry some risks relating to over-reliance, but has the potential to improve the quality of case recording and care planning.

Improving how families, carers and individuals engage with services

Implemented appropriately, with effective guardrails, AI has the potential to improve how citizens engage with social care services. For example, it has the potential to:

support plain-English explanations of assessments, plans and the statutory process

reduce power imbalances by improving how families and individuals understand statutory frameworks and the experience, support or care they are likely to receive

enable children, parents, carers and people who draw on care to access records in a more appropriate and compassionate way

analyse service user feedback to improve services

enable tools to support citizens to understand what support may be available.

capture the thoughts, feelings, aspirations and challenges a child, family, carer or individual drawing on care may face

Some of these use cases are still emerging in social care and should be evaluated before wider adoption.

Evaluation should consider:

accuracy

accessibility

equality

user experience

data protection

information governance

whether the tool improves people’s ability to understand, participate in and shape their care and support

Improving access to services

AI’s ability to process natural language and generate accurate responses when trained on trusted, approved information and advice is improving how citizens access services.

With appropriate governance and safeguards, chatbots are being used to help citizens access the support and solutions they need. Translation capabilities increase equality of access – having access available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week reduces barriers to getting the right support.

Case study: Bradford Council – supporting adult social care front door with AI digital assistants

Bradford Council has introduced a digital assistant, ‘Annie’, accessed online or through WhatsApp. Annie offers a new access channel available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week – helping people get the right information at the right time. Annie operates from a ‘locked box’. This means that it is specifically trained on trusted, approved information and advice from content that is curated by the council. It can process over 40 languages across both text inputs and voice notes, reducing barriers to use and services.

Built into Annie is the concept that if a person asks more than 4 questions, they probably have a complex situation, need to talk to a human and are directed to the ‘front door’. Behind Annie there is an active monitoring layer which flags any potential safeguarding issues. Users are advised not to enter personal information through the user interface. If any personal data is shared, this is identified and redacted in the backend.

Bradford Council: supporting the ASC front door with AI digital assistants has more information.

Some of these use cases are yet to be explored in a social care context, but they are being seen across other sectors. They should be carefully evaluated before adoption, regularly reviewed and monitored for the accuracy of outputs and the governance and protection of information.

Limitations on AI use

Where AI should not be used

Engagement with local authorities and other sector organisations highlights that it would be helpful to know where AI should not be used in practice. DfE’s view is that AI, in its current form, should be approached with significant extra caution or avoided in the following high-risk or high-consequence situations.

AI alone should not determine risk, need, eligibility, safeguarding thresholds or interventions, or independently make or suggest decisions that directly affect an individual, child, young person or family

AI cannot properly understand context, nuance or inference, and decisions should remain with practitioners. For example, AI should not determine what intervention should be taken in a case. AI may support practitioners by organising information, identifying possible patterns, highlighting gaps or inconsistencies and prompting further professional enquiry, helping practitioners consider risk systematically and decide what further information or action may be needed.

Directly recording into case records and care planning without meaningful human oversight

This may lead to inaccuracies perpetuating throughout case records and ultimately presenting an inaccurate version of events.

Making an independent assessment of individual needs or risks that are not subject to the reflections and judgement of the practitioner

AI tools should not be making independent assessments of risks or care and support needs. They are better placed in helping the practitioner gather, summarise and process evidence to help them make their professionally informed assessment of needs or risks. Predictive tools may support strategic planning or professional enquiry but should not determine decisions affecting individuals without professional judgement and oversight.

Where AI should be used with caution

Making predictions about individual needs

Although some AI tools can use predictive analytics to process large amounts of data and generate forecasts and predictions on an individual’s likely needs, caution should be used when considering whether to use this capability.

If AI tools are being used for predictive analytics, organisations should ensure models are well-documented and understood, tested for accuracy and bias, and subject to ongoing evaluation to assess their impact and effectiveness.

Automating elements of processes and workflows

AI, particularly Agentic AI (for example an AI model that is capable of completing tasks independently or alongside other AI models) has the potential to streamline workflows and automate processes.

Agentic AI could reduce time spent on:

communication

administrative tasks

information retrieval

Use caution to ensure that this is appropriate, accurate, and does not undermine the professional integrity of practitioners.

A lower-risk use may include using simple agents to support practitioners to challenge their reasoning and reflect on their practice.

A more cautious and considered approach may be needed when using agentic AI for more complex cases, such as directly engaging with people who draw on care or completing workflows within case management and care planning systems.

Robust local governance, feedback loops and policies should be in place to safeguard quality, consistency and accuracy. Agentic AI may need to:

be grounded in specific, context-relevant content

operate within clearly defined instructions and boundaries

remain subject to meaningful human oversight and intervention

A range of tools and guides are available to help public sector bodies govern and openly document their use of AI, including the:

Responsible AI Toolkit

AI Risk Management Toolkit

Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS)

Supporting or assisting with triage of cases

There are examples of AI being effectively used to support and assist with triaging cases. Caution should be used to ensure that:

AI models are not making decisions that will impact the care or wellbeing of individuals without meaningful human oversight

organisations understand the accuracy and limitations of the model, including any potential for bias

consideration is given to how oversight is maintained, including for example, through auditability of individuals’ journeys through the ‘system’

Predictive analytics, AI-enabled strategic insights and triage tools may support strategic planning, prioritisation for professional review or the identification of issues for human consideration.

Some of the greatest value of these uses of AI comes from helping practitioners or leaders ask better questions, identify patterns and target further enquiry. They should not determine outcomes for individuals without practitioner judgement, governance and meaningful human oversight.

There are examples across government and the public sector where AI-assisted decision making is proving effective:

the NHS is proving AI’s ability to support with diagnosis and medical image interpretation

policing is using facial recognition and digital forensics to support CCTV analysis and sorting through digital evidence

some local authorities are using AI to improve waste collections and streamline customer services

This reflects the current position of AI, and its use in children’s and adult social care. We will continue to review and revisit this as evidence emerges and technology continues to develop.

Ethics, risks and challenges of AI

AI offers a range of opportunities to support practitioners and the social care sector but brings a set of new risks, challenges and ethical considerations. Some of these stem from the way AI models are developed and work, others from how we interact with them. For example, over-reliance on AI outputs and reduced professional judgement may degrade decision-making.

The use of AI may, at times, involve trade-offs between potential benefits and ethical values. These should be:

documented

governed transparently

considered with practitioners and people affected by the system, where appropriate

The rise of easily accessible AI in recent years introduces vulnerabilities that extend beyond the ethical questions and risks raised in this guidance. For example, the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse highlights that AI is being used to create artificial child sexual abuse material and manipulate still or moving images of individuals.

Annex A has information on ethical considerations, risks and challenges and potential mitigations, alongside a checklist for practitioners.

Considerations for the appropriate use of AI

The following section sets out some of the main considerations for the appropriate use of AI in children’s and adult social care. Many of these are not specific to the sector but carry more importance due to the sensitivity of ‘data’ relating to people who draw on care, children, families and carers supported through social care and the potential impacts of decisions made with (and without) the use of AI.

AI tools should work within an interconnected system where the individual, child, young person or family is at the heart, and the practitioner is responsible and accountable.

Governance

We recommend that local authorities and social care organisations should have, or be working to implement, governance arrangements for the use of AI in frontline practice. This should extend beyond corporate level governance and should be reflective of the high-risk and high-consequence nature of social care and how AI works as a technology.

Without effective governance, oversight and accountability remain vague. This can reduce the effectiveness of AI and increase the organisational risks associated with inappropriate use of AI. Organisations may want to provide clarity (for example through clear and accessible policies) for practitioners on what tools can be used and for what purposes.

Robust governance of AI tools should consider:

data governance – for example, where data processed by AI tools sits and retention periods

people governance such as:

usage policies

impacts on practice

human oversight and meaningful human control

training and learning

Main points for organisations

Effective governance should, as a minimum:

identify and manage ethical, legal, safeguarding and operational risks

assess and manage data protection implications, including legal bases for AI use in the collection and processing of data

set clear rules on approved, restricted and prohibited use (for example AI usage policy)

support staff to understand how AI may and may not be used

establish approaches to training and supervision and oversight

define roles, responsibilities and escalation routes

provide assurance, monitoring and review arrangements, and escalation routes

include procurement and supplier assurance

clarify:

consent

agreements

transparency arrangements

Annex B includes a governance checklist intended to help organisations assess their approach to governing AI tools in social care.

AI tools should comply with relevant legislation and regulation, including data protection legislation. Local authorities and organisations should also align with established transparency and data protection standards (such as Article 5 of UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)).

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has published guidance on AI and data protection.

Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) from Government Digital Service helps public sector organisations to publish information about the algorithmic tools they are using and why they are using them.

AI Readiness and self-assessment

Organisations that have not yet started to adopt AI or are at an early stage of their AI journey, may find it helpful to assess their readiness before adopting or scaling AI tools in children’s and adult social care. This includes considering whether they have the right governance, data protection arrangements, technical infrastructure, workforce capability, leadership and assurance in place to use AI safely and effectively.

Local authorities can use the Adult Social Care Assessments Improvement Toolkit Self-assessment Tool to help identify areas of their practice that could be improved through digital and AI-enabled solutions.

The AI Readiness framework and checklist was developed by Bright (the Birmingham AI & Digital Health and Care Group based at the University of Birmingham and University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust) as part of their AI Readiness Project.

It:

provides a practical framework to support organisations in health and care settings to consider these issues

can help organisations identify strengths, gaps and areas for further development before implementing AI in practice

The AI Playbook for the UK government and AI Knowledge Hub provides additional guidance on how to govern AI programmes and initiatives.

Implementation and monitoring

AI adoption should be treated as a change programme, rather than a ‘traditional’ technology rollout. It needs ongoing support, clear messaging, visible leadership, workforce capability-building and opportunities for practitioners to shape and test tools. This helps ensure tools reflect user needs, increasing effectiveness and maximising the benefit for the organisation and the citizens they support.

Organisations should consider how to continue to develop the right capabilities and culture to enable the safe use of AI in frontline practice. This could include hands-on training, simple guidance, GDPR and data governance workshops, acceptable use policies, peer learning, AI champions and feedback loops for sharing good practice, issues and concerns.

AI tools are not static. Both the tools themselves, and the models they are built on are likely to be constantly developing and evolving. Reflecting this, organisations should be aware of updates and factor ongoing monitoring in their deployment and adoption of AI, using appropriate governance and oversight arrangements as tools and their use develop.

Case study: Brent Council’s system approach to implementing AI in practice

Brent Council’s children’s social care set out to implement AI in a way that really supports practice: reducing administrative pressure, improving access to information, and creating more time for meaningful work with children and families. The aim was clear: AI should enhance practice, not replace professional judgement.

Approach

Brent’s children’s social care department took a coordinated and carefully governed approach. Practitioners, managers, practice leaders, learning and development colleagues, digital services and information governance teams worked together to ensure AI was introduced with the right safeguards, training and oversight. This balanced approach has helped staff explore the benefits of AI while staying aligned with Brent’s values, responsibilities and ‘Ways of Working’ (Brent’s practice framework).

Impact

Staff report greater confidence in using AI safely, responsibly and purposefully.

Practitioners are spending less time on drafting, summarising and routine administrative tasks.

Teams are creating more capacity for direct, relationship-based work with children and families.

Managers have additional capacity to support reflective supervision, quality assurance and service improvement ideas.

Improvements in the department’s understanding of safe, ethical use of AI.

Organisations should be supporting their practitioners to develop their understanding of and confidence in using AI tools.

Robust learning and development offers should both consider tool-specific training and courses and modules on the AI in its broader sense. This may help practitioners understand how AI works, and its limitations – underlining the importance of:

reviewing outputs

the ‘human in the loop’

retaining professional judgement

avoiding over reliance

Supporting practitioners to develop their AI skills and maturity can help ensure the value of AI tools is increased.

How to Test and Evaluate AI has useful prompts for organisations to consider when implementing and monitoring AI tools.

Case study: Essex County Council’s adult social care approach to implementation

When exploring the implementation of AI in adult social care, a proof-of-concept tested AI transcription and summarisation in adult social care practice produced learning that was relevant to the whole organisation.

It showed how AI can support practice while also highlighting the conditions required to use AI safely, legally and confidently across the organisation.

What Essex County Council learned:

AI can improve clarity, reduce recording burden and support presence in conversations when strong human oversight is in place

secure purpose-built tools performed best for high-risk statutory work

secure general-purpose tools are useful for low risk

Lawful data processing

Article 5 of UK GDPR sets out seven main principles for data protection:

lawfulness

fairness and transparency

purpose limitation

data minimisation

accuracy

storage limitation

integrity and confidentiality (security)

accountability

These should be considered when implementing and adopting AI in children’s social care to provide the foundations for good data protection practice.

When processing personal data, whether AI is being used or not, a legal basis under Article 6 of the UK GDPR must be identified. Additionally, where that personal data is special category data (such as health data, racial or ethnic origin and sexual orientation), at least one of the conditions in Article 9 must be satisfied.

The common law duty of confidentiality (CLDC) must also be considered. More information is available from the duty of confidentiality.

The basic principle underlying the CLDC is that a person who receives information in confidence must not take unfair advantage of it or use or disclose it to the prejudice of the confider without consent.

In the absence of consent, the CLDC may be overridden on the basis of legal requirement, statutory power or overriding public interest.

Where automated processing is being used to make individual decisions, organisations must also consider whether the provisions in Section 4A of Chapter III of the UK GDPR apply. These provisions apply where automated processing is used to make a significant decision without meaningful human involvement in the taking of the decision.

Organisations should ensure that they have identified the relevant legal power and undertaken the analysis set out above when using AI and reflect this in their guidance and documentation as part of their implementation and governance approaches.

Ultimately, it is your responsibility to ensure you comply with all data protection legislation, and organisations may want to consider how they support practitioner compliance.

Trust and choice

Trust is fundamental to effective social care, and this should not be jeopardised by using AI or any other tool.

Organisations should support their frontline staff to understand the organisation’s policies on being transparent and what to do when people disagree to the use of AI when working with people who draw on care. This includes:

children

young people and families

people who may not be able to disagree themselves, for example during mental capacity assessments

This may include providing clear and accessible guidance and policies on transparency and the choices people have about the use of AI in practice and how to handle objections. This should be in line with data protection law, safeguarding responsibilities and local, organisational policy.

If practitioners understand their organisation’s policies on choice, and are able to explain the tools they use, this may help to:

build trust with individuals, children, young people, families and partner organisations

ensure alignment with data protection and safeguarding obligations

give individuals the opportunity to object to its use

There may be times when those families or individuals will not agree to AI being used in their care and support. They are within their rights to do so, and organisations should ensure that there are clear alternative processes in place for where individuals refuse permission to use AI.

When used with other organisations (for example in multi-agency meetings), it may be worth considering how agreement to use AI can be addressed through governance or at an organisational level. This is most likely to be relevant when using AI for recording or minuting meetings.

Practitioners should ensure that they adhere to different organisations’ policies on AI when working in partnership with them.

Transparency

Organisations should support transparency by ensuring staff understand what tools are in use, what they do, where they may be used, and how outputs should be used and reviewed. Where appropriate, organisations should also support practitioners to explain AI use clearly to children, families, carers, individuals and partner agencies.

This can be supported by ensuring practitioners:

understand, at a non-technical level, the AI tools that they are using, and how the output is generated

can explain how AI will be used in their practice, and outputs reviewed, to individuals, children, families and partner organisations where appropriate

can explain why AI is being used, understand where and when it can be used and the limitations and hard boundaries

understand when people should be informed and can disagree to the use of AI

are clear on how objections to AI use should be managed

understand and follow relevant organisational guidance

can feedback issues and challenges and share learning and practice with peers

are supported by organisational transparency about systems in use

Organisations may find the following resources useful for providing plain English guidance to staff around AI to support organisational transparency:

use of clear language

guidance and standards on plain English

Organisations may also want to consider how they can provide transparency more generally on the use of AI in social care, for example through accessible information for the public.

Buying and deploying tools appropriately

Organisations should use this policy paper, alongside wider advice and guidance, to create the conditions in which practitioners feel confident and supported to use AI:

appropriately

ethically

in the best interests of children, families and people who draw on care without diminishing their professional judgement and discretion

Organisations are responsible for creating the conditions for safe, appropriate and lawful use of AI. This should include:

procuring safe and secure tools

approving use cases for tools, and innovations

providing staff with appropriate, engaging and accurate guidance that is updated to reflect emerging AI technologies as they are implemented

providing training on tools and necessary capabilities

reviewing AI use and impact

challenging inappropriate use and escalating where necessary.

This should address both how individuals use AI tools and how organisations decide which tools to develop or procure. For local government, councils can use the Local Government Association (LGA) guide on responsibly buying AI.

When procuring AI tools, organisations should consider and assess tools based on their functionality and security.

Consider asking more grounded questions about what the tool actually does, and whether it is focused on an area where AI can be beneficial.

Grounding

Where possible, organisations may want to consider grounding AI tools with authoritative and relevant source material.

Grounding refers to providing an AI system with trusted information and evidence on which to base its response, helping to reduce the risk of inaccurate, incomplete or fabricated outputs. Several of the case studies outlined in this guidance reflect the benefit of grounding AI tools in authoritative material, such as national statutory or non-statutory guidance and local guidance or policies.

Grounding does not guarantee accuracy. Practitioners should continue to review and verify AI-generated outputs and apply professional judgements.

Case study: North Yorkshire Council ‘Policy Buddy’

Focused on a practical challenge practitioners face every day: finding the right information quickly to inform professional practice, North Yorkshire introduced an AI-powered knowledge assistant ‘Policy Buddy’ to help children’s social care practitioners quickly access and interpret policies, procedures, statutory guidance and legislation.

The tool is built on local and statutory guidance and designed to only provide factual information rather than recommendations, ensuring professional judgement remains with social workers.

Over 800 practitioners were using ‘Policy Buddy’ in the first 3 months of implementation. The evaluation found that:

practitioners can save 5 to 7 hours each week

there were increases in practice consistency and professional confidence

managers reported improved compliance

Find out more about Policy Buddy .

Innovation

Some local authorities and social care organisations are innovating with use cases for AI, either on their own or in collaboration with private or third sector organisations to solve practice-led problems.

DfE and DHSC support responsible innovation in the use of AI, provided that it is accompanied by appropriate safeguards, governance and oversight, and that organisations are mindful of the risks and ethics associated with the use of AI.

Organisations are responsible for ensuring compliance with all relevant legislation and statutory guidance such as:

data protection legislation (including the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018)

Care Act 2014

Children Act 1989

Children Act 2004

Working together to safeguard children

Case study: Peterborough City Council’s ‘Hey Geraldine’

In Peterborough Council, staff frequently relied on a highly experienced occupational therapist for advice, creating bottlenecks and limiting access to expertise.

AI Solution

They developed ‘Hey Geraldine’, a bespoke AI assistant trained on the knowledge of an experienced practitioner, to provide instant guidance to staff.

Outcome

‘Hey Geraldine’ answered over 1,200 questions and saved around 15 minutes per interaction, freeing staff to focus on more complex work. This demonstrates how AI can scale access to specialist knowledge and expert advice without increasing staff workload and resource.

The quality of tools developed ‘in-house’ are likely to depend on the quality of the underlying data and how easily it can be accessed and shared across systems. AI will not compensate for incomplete, inconsistent or poorly structured information. When considering innovation, it may be worth considering wider data and information readiness alongside AI readiness.

Organisations should be aware that some AI systems’ capability to generate web apps via prompts is enabling individuals to create apps and tools without prior knowledge or experience.

This may result in the development of solutions to real-world problems, but consideration should be given to how secure these tools might be. Many of these apps are likely to be hosted by the generating product (both OpenAI and Claude currently offer this functionality) and may not be covered by the organisations’ secure environments or enterprise agreements.

Considerations for practitioners and organisations

The following sections set out the main considerations that are relevant to practitioners in using AI to support frontline practice, and organisations in supporting the safe use of AI.

Annex C has a checklist to help practitioners consider these aspects when using AI.

The role of the practitioner

AI tools offer great opportunities to support practitioners and their use should be guided by:

transparency

the ‘human in the loop’

the principle that professional judgement remains with practitioners

organisational policies and guidance

Final decisions on any aspect of casework decision-making relating to children, young people, families and people who draw on care should be made by the practitioner (alongside partner agencies where relevant). The practitioner is ultimately accountable for their casework.

Where AI tools are being used to support frontline practice, it is important that practitioners’ own thoughts, judgements and assessments are reflected in the final content.

This can be the difference between an accurate assessment of need and an AI-generated output that lacks context and human analysis. AI tools cannot understand body language, tone and inflections or accurately weight information in order of importance (relevant to the context).

Case records, care planning and related documentation should reflect the wider engagement, rather than just a summary of a direct transcript or other AI generated content. Where appropriate, practitioners should allow the child, family, carer or person drawing on care to have sight of the AI transcript or summary produced for them to ensure their voice and needs have been accurately captured.

It is expected that practitioners using AI to generate content will:

check the content for basic accuracy including spelling, grammar, conversation accuracy

carefully review the output to prevent bias and hallucinations (generation of outputs that are inaccurate, misleading or incorrect) and ensure it is contextually accurate

ensure, where appropriate, the output is amended to include additional information or analysis that AI tools cannot pick up on, for example body language, tone, facial expressions, physical observations

adhere to their organisation’s AI usage policy where relevant

Close attention should be paid to outputs that will be included or used in:

case records

documentation or care planning

legal or statutory settings

Main point for practitioners

AI outputs should always be treated as a first draft, not a final answer. Case records and reports should reflect practitioner thinking, critical reflection and professional judgement.

AI can be more effective when practitioners develop their own critical reflections and judgements before using AI to generate a first draft, so they can interrogate the draft from an informed place. Think first, then draft.

Reviewing drafts should be considered a professional task, rather than a proof-reading exercise. Practitioners should test whether content is accurate, evidenced, balanced and reflective of their own judgement. Practitioners will need to add things AI cannot capture, including observations, context, uncertainty, professional curiosity and the significance of what was not said as well as what was.

Accountability

Local authorities and social care organisations should support their practitioners to understand accountability for the use of AI. This could be through specific training and local guidance. Managers can support this by providing oversight and ensuring that their teams understand how to use AI appropriately and safely.

Clear accountability is essential to ensuring the safe, appropriate and effective use of AI in social care:

practitioners remain accountable for their work, the decisions they make and should be able to justify their decisions

managers are accountable for supervision and oversight

organisations remain accountable for the governance, policy and assurance that enables the safe and appropriate use of AI

Ensuring accuracy

AI may present opportunities to help identify inaccuracies and biases that individuals may be prone to. Used well, it can also help identify inconsistencies and errors and highlight evidence gaps.

AI-generated outputs and content, however, may be inaccurate, incomplete, misleading or overly confident. They reflect the underlying model or the user’s prompt and are prone to confidently presenting incorrect information as fact, sometimes oversimplifying complex situations or downplaying risks.

They will return a credible response unless told otherwise and are, therefore, vulnerable to hallucinations and inaccuracies. A helpful point to remember here is that AI models and tools do not understand the outputs they are generating.

These risks do not remove the potential value of AI but do underline the need for careful review and oversight, ensuring any gaps are filled and inaccuracies corrected before use in a professional context.

Practitioners, supervisors and managers should be mindful that recording inaccuracies can have both short- and long-term consequences. Inaccuracies in the short-term may result in missed opportunities to achieve a positive outcome.

In the long-term, inaccuracies may be reiterated, becoming seen as the ‘truth’. They have enduring implications for the child, young person, family, or person drawing on care and their understanding of events and relationships when accessing and looking back over their records in the future.

Prompting: asking the right questions

Many GenAI tools (those that generate new outputs) rely on prompts to shape the output. Some GenAI tools that develop outputs to meet a specific purpose may also have prompts built in.

Clearer instructions usually result in better outputs to use as a first draft.

Main point for practitioners

Good prompts ask the tool to summarise evidence. Poor prompts ask the tool to make professional judgements.

Well prompted AI tools should support record-writing, not determine needs, risks, eligibility, safeguarding concerns or other statutory decisions.

Practitioners remain responsible for reviewing, editing and approving all outputs before they are added to case records.

Where organisations choose to support the use of GenAI tools, they may find it helpful to provide staff with simple prompting frameworks to improve quality. A frequent example used in a public sector context is the GCSE framework:

Goal: clearly define what you want the AI to accomplish

Context: provide background information so the AI understands the purpose and audience

Source: specify where the AI should retrieve information from

Expectation: describe the desired format, tone, style, or length of the output

Ensuring safety and data privacy

AI is a data-driven tool. As a sector, we need to be mindful of the data protection and safety risks when procuring, implementing, governing or using AI.

Organisations should define clearly which tools are approved for use, what categories of information may be entered into them, and what safeguards apply.

A general guide is included here, but organisations may have more specific stances.

Publicly accessible AI platforms

Platforms that have not been procured as part of an organisation’s corporate licensing are not secure. No personal, identifiable or case-specific information should be put into these tools. Information entered may be stored, processed or reused by the tool. Many of these AI systems may learn from this data, and any information entered could be replicated elsewhere, creating a data breach.

Corporately licensed tools

For example Microsoft Copilot as part of an organisation’s Microsoft 365 package. These tools are generally more secure but may still have some data protection implications if inputs are used to train the organisation-specific model. Personal information could potentially resurface elsewhere in the organisation through a response to a prompt. If a corporate GenAI assistant is being considered for use in social care, corporate usage policies should clearly state the limitations on use.

Use-case-specific-tools, procured for a specific purpose

For example a social care specific transcription tool. These tools are likely to be more secure, and in many cases are less likely to use data entered into them for training and development.

We recommend that organisations develop a simple way to help practitioners understand what data can be entered into which tool as this will vary based on the procurement and contractual arrangements.

More information on AI data protection principles and risks is available from the National Cyber Security Centre: ChatGPT and LLMs: what’s the risk and Principles for security of Machine learning ML.

Main point for practitioners and organisations

AI tools included in corporate packages may not include the necessary guardrails to guarantee data protection of personal information.

We recommend that organisations provide clarity on whether corporate AI tools have the necessary protections in place to effectively protect personal information in line with:

data protection regulations

security requirements

local policies

If in doubt, check – if you are still in doubt, do not add personal information to the tool.

The regulators’ positions on AI

Ofsted’s position on the use of AI

Ofsted supports innovation and the use of AI where it improves the education and care of children.

Ofsted do not look at AI as a stand-alone part of our inspections, and do not directly evaluate the use of AI, nor of any AI tool. However, inspectors can consider the impact that the use of AI has on the outcomes and experiences of children and learners. That includes both how providers themselves use AI, and how they respond to the use of AI by others – for example parents, children and learners.

Similarly, Ofsted do not consider the use of AI in and of itself in their regulation practice. However, Ofsted’s evaluation of the impact of AI use in regulated settings may be used to help inform any enforcement action.

Ofsted do not require their inspectors to actively look for AI use, and their inspection reports will not refer to AI unless it is crucial to their broader inspection and regulatory decisions. If inspectors find that a provider’s use of, and response to AI has a significant impact on children and learners, they will record it in the same way as any other evidence gathered during inspection.

Ofsted do not expect inspectors to understand how AI software has been designed – any more than, for example, they need to understand the programming of a provider’s firewall software to evaluate their data security arrangements.

How Ofsted looks at AI during inspection and regulation has more information.

Social Work England’s position on AI

Social Work England recognises the potential benefits of AI in social work practice. Where appropriate, social workers can use artificial intelligence (AI) as a tool to support, rather than replace, their professional judgment and values. AI should be used in a way that strengthens ethical, reflective, and relationship-based practice consistent with the core values underpinning Social Work England’s professional standards.

Social workers remain accountable for their decisions and the quality of their practice, regardless of whether AI tools are used, in line with the professional standards. Emerging technology, such as AI can support human judgement, but it should never replace it.

Where AI is used, it is essential that practitioners critically evaluate AI outputs, recognising that these tools can reflect biases and inaccuracies. Social workers are responsible for ensuring that:

any tools comply with legal and organisational standards

those they work with understand how the tool is being used

any use of AI is always aligned with ethical practice

Ongoing digital literacy and critical reflection are essential for ethical AI use in social work. Practitioners should understand both the capabilities and limitations of AI, as well as opportunities to reflect on its impact on practice and people with lived experience.

Care Quality Commission’s (CQC) position on the use of AI

As England’s independent regulator of health and social care, the CQC encourages the use of innovative technologies, including AI, where the technology benefits people and results in more effective and efficient services. However, it acknowledges that AI is not without risk and the use of AI should contribute to safe, equitable and person-centred care.

The CQC:

recognises that AI is rapidly expanding across health and social care, offering clear benefits, for example efficiency, earlier risk identification, improved monitoring, but also significant risks

does not regulate specific AI tools but ensures that existing regulations are applied so AI supports safe, effective, equitable and person‑centred care

expects providers to use AI responsibly, with human oversight, transparency, accountability, and strong governance, ensuring it enhances – not replaces – professional judgement

will integrate AI into its regulatory approach, support innovation, and continue developing guidance to help the sector use AI safely and effectively

Artificial intelligence in health and social care: CQC’s role, expectations and plans has more information.
