Glossary: types of AI

AI is a broad and open term used to encompass a range of technologies. These technologies often work together in AI tools – for example transcription tools often draw on ‘Ambient Voice Technology’, Natural Language Processing and GenAI.

Most AI tools currently used in social care are based on machine learning models. These models are trained on large amounts of data to recognise patterns and generate outputs. Rather than understanding information in the way humans do, they identify relationships in data and produce responses that are likely to be relevant based on their training.

Some machine learning models, known as deep learning models, are able to learn complex patterns from large datasets, making them capable of speech recognition, image analysis and generative AI.

Common AI use cases

Speech recognition (SR) also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR) and ambient voice technology (AVT)

A technology that converts spoken audio into text (or speech-to-speech). Often referred to as ‘transcription’ and sits alongside GenAI to create summarised transcriptions and populate templates.

Computer vision (CV)

AI that interprets images and video by analysing pixels to detect and classify objects, people and scenes – for example medical imaging, surveillance, robotics.

Natural language processing (NLP)

Techniques that represent language numerically so models can understand, analyse and generate text – for example translation, sentiment, chatbots.

Generative AI (GenAI)

Models trained on large datasets that generate new text, images, audio or video by sampling learned patterns – for example content creation and modelling. Some GenAI tools include the ability to develop ‘agents’ to complete/support with simple tasks.

Agentic AI

Systems or ‘agents’ built on foundation models that can plan, decide and act using tools to achieve goals with minimal human input. These can be task-specific agents, workflow agents or tool-using agents. Different types of agents specialising in completing different tasks might be used together to automate end-to-end processes. It is worth noting this differs from ‘AI Agents’ – these are more likely to be GenAI-centred assistants, like chatbots.

Across the children’s and adult social care sector, we are most readily seeing Speech Recognition, Natural Language Processing and GenAI used. These technologies work together in the case of transcription tools to provide summaries of discussions and meetings.

Annex A: ethics, risks and challenges of AI

A summary of some of the ethical risks and challenges associated with the use of AI, and examples of how these risks might be mitigated.

Professional judgement and human oversight

AI undermines professional integrity, judgement and ethical decision-making.

Reduced critical thinking and over-reliance on AI outputs, leading to poorer practice and recording.

AI tools may be prone to automation bias, meaning outputs are given undue trust or weight because the tool appears authoritative.

Mitigating the risks

AI should be used to support (not replace) professional judgement (used well AI can support practice, learning and help practitioners extend their capability) but the practitioner remains responsible for decisions and final records and should be applying their own analysis and reflections to AI output where appropriate.

Practitioners may want to first ask themselves what their own critical reflection of the situation is, so they can interrogate an AI generated draft from an informed place and to mitigate against authority bias.

AI outputs should be treated as a first draft: review, edit and add your own analysis, reflections, judgements and context before use.

Robust audit arrangements, alongside post-deployment monitoring, on the use of AI will strengthen the organisation’s oversight of AI use and the application of professional judgement.

Over-reliance and deskilling

Practitioners may come to rely too much on AI rather than professional judgement.

Over-reliance on AI may lead to practitioners losing or not fully developing (in the case of new entry practitioners) their analytical, reflective and critical thinking skills.

Mitigating the risk

AI should be used to strengthen practice, not replace it. Good practice in social care relies on professional judgements, and we should be using AI in a way that supports and complements this, rather than replaces it.

Accountability and governance

AI outputs are accepted without challenge, leading to errors being recorded within documentation and practitioners not taking ownership of their decisions.

Mitigating the risk

Organisations should be clear on accountability and governance and ensure that practitioners are clear on where accountability sits. Managers and supervisors should be aware of their responsibility for overseeing AI within practice.

Audit arrangements should factor in and account for the use of AI and support managers and supervisors to identify where practitioners might be inappropriately using AI.

Accuracy and hallucination

AI produces incorrect (but often plausible) or incomplete content, including misunderstandings of transcripts or context.

AI may also infer conclusions from the conversations that are inaccurate or false. These are often presented with confidence by the AI.

AI may also produce a coherent summary that discourages further questioning.

Inaccuracies and hallucinations, left unchecked, misinform decision-making.

Hallucinations are a feature of AI tools, and not a bug. The risk of hallucinations cannot be entirely eliminated but can be mitigated against.

Mitigating the risk

Outputs should be verified against source information and amended before saving; AI text should not be copied into records unchecked by a practitioner.

Any conclusions included within outputs should be reviewed and tested for accuracy. Practitioners may want to consider how prompting can reduce inferences.

Practitioners should feel confident in challenging and testing AI outputs, reducing the risk of AI impeding critical thinking and professional curiosity. Practitioners and the individuals and families they support should be cognisant that AI is not infallible, and outputs should be tested and challenged for inaccuracies. Practitioners should also consider the implications of errors being included in the final document when reviewing.

AI can be prompted to give a confidence rating on its outputs. This may help understand the initial accuracy of outputs.

Bias, unfair treatment, fairness and equity

AI systems may reflect or amplify patterns of bias present in training data, design choices or deployment context. This can often be in ways that are difficult to detect. This creates risk of unfair treatment, distorted analysis or unequal impacts on different groups.

This means AI may exacerbate existing inequalities, including gender and racial bias, and can sometimes influence how GenAI responds.

Research has found some AI tools produce different summaries depending on individual characteristics, such as gender. Examples include men’s needs being described more directly, while women’s needs were sometimes less clear or under-emphasised.

Mitigating the risk

Practitioners and managers should be alert to bias when reviewing AI outputs, as this can affect how needs are understood and acted on, and should not rely on AI alone. Outputs should be checked carefully and anything that seems unclear, biased or unfair should be questioned.

Where AI is used at scale, organisations should test and monitor tools or models for bias, fairness and unequal impact, and take actions where issues are identified.

Organisations should ensure they:

have robust equalities impact assessments in place (including Public Sector Equalities Duty (PSED) and Human Rights checks)

follow internal policies

set clear expectations for practitioners to review outputs for accuracy, fairness and alignment with professional judgement and value

Where concerns arise, feedback loops can help ensure that these issues are addressed and understood by peers.

Transparency, explainability and trust

AI may be used without staff understanding how it works, its limitations, or how data is handled. This can impact their ability to clearly explain how tools are being used and how content will be reviewed.

There are risks around the explainability of AI tools themselves. It is often unclear how AI tools have generated their outputs.

Using AI without explanation (or consent or agreement in certain situations) may damage trust in both the practitioners and the organisation.

Mitigating the risk

Practitioners should be clear about when and why AI is used. Steps should be taken to ensure users understand limitations and remain accountable for outputs.

Practitioners should be able to explain both the tool they are using and how outputs will be used and next steps. They should be supported to develop a basic understanding of how AI works and organisations should provide clear, accessible guidance to help practitioners understand the tools they use.

Organisations should have clear local policies and guidance to outline:

the way that AI is used

what staff need to be aware of

how they can escalate issues and concerns within the local authority

Practitioner confidence will help grow trust in the use of AI in practice. Organisations should support practitioners to develop their AI skills to both confidently use, and explain the use of, AI in their practice.

Privacy, security and data protection

Personal and sensitive information may be unintentionally shared (through prompts or AI outputs) or stored and reused by third‑party tools, risking data protection and security breaches and creating uncertainty about ownership and Intellectual Property.

Mitigating the risk

Only approved tools should be used, and personal or case data should not be entered into publicly available AI tools. Corporately purchased tools should confirm storage, retention and training use. Anyone using AI should follow their organisation’s data protection guidance and organisations should keep terms up to date.

Organisations should have clear local policies and data protection impact assessments (DPIAs) which outline:

the way that AI is used and data is processed

what staff need to be aware of

how they can escalate issues or concerns within the local authority

AI in multi-disciplinary settings

Different organisations may have different policies on how and when AI can be used. This can lead to situations where AI cannot be used.

Mitigating the risk

AI use should be agreed upon prior to meetings including more than one organisation.

Partner organisations may also want to agree what use of AI will be accepted in evidence or assessment and planning documentation. Where AI has been used, any decision-making and professional judgement should remain with the practitioner, and it would remain their responsibility if there were any complaints or court proceedings.

Legal risk

If invalid or incorrect AI outputs are left unchecked and used to produce legal effects on a person within statutory decision-making or to different outcomes than would have otherwise occurred, this could lead to:

legal repercussions for the local authority or professional responsible

long-term impacts on the child, family or individual drawing on care

This risk is particularly relevant where there is statutory decision-making.

Mitigating the risk

Practitioners should ensure they read and check AI outputs for accuracy and should not use AI tools to make decisions. They are responsible for the AI-generated content and should be able to justify reasoning.

Organisations may wish to take extra care when supporting newly qualified practitioners, including through learning, development and supervision. Local authorities may want to consider how AI is factored in as part of learning, development and training – including how to both critique AI outputs and use AI to enhance critical thinking.

AI Drift

An AI model’s performance may get worse over time because the world it is working in has changed. For example it keeps using historical data, and does not update to reflect current data, new policies and processes or external events. This means the model’s assumptions and outputs are no longer as accurate.

Mitigating the risk

Practitioners should ensure they continue to check outputs for accuracy and ensure external factors (that the AI may not be aware of) are considered.

Organisations should ensure they are aware of updates and patches to tools and that these are clearly communicated. Organisations should be aware that updates and patches to AI systems and tools are not always unambiguously beneficial. For example, an update may enable a tool to make or advise on a decision where the previous version did not. Organisations should also ensure that any data inputs are as accurate as possible.

Annex B: organisational governance checklist for AI in social care

Purpose

Use this checklist to establish proportionate organisational oversight and assurance across the AI lifecycle. Record your answers, evidence, accountable owner and review date.

This is intended to provide a starting point for organisations to build upon to reflect their own situation, organisational needs and established governance.

Proportionate assurance

Set the level of scrutiny according to the sensitivity of the data, the degree of autonomy and the potential impact on people, practice or statutory functions. Higher risk uses may require enhanced multidisciplinary review, senior approval, stronger auditability and more frequent monitoring. The AI Risk Management Tool Kit provides advice on implementing a simple tiered approach – children’s safeguarding and statutory uses should be considered as high-consequence by default.

AI should not make autonomous decisions about assessment, risk, need, eligibility, safeguarding, care planning or intervention, or write unchecked content into case records.

1. Governance structure and accountability

A senior responsible owner is accountable for the organisation’s AI approach, with named operational, information governance, security and practice owners.

A defined governance forum has authority to approve, condition, reject, pause or withdraw AI tools and use cases.

Terms of reference set decision rights, membership, quorum, reporting arrangements, escalation routes and review frequency.

An AI policy defines approved, restricted and prohibited uses, required controls, practitioner accountability and exceptions.

A central register records every tool and use case, supplier, purpose, data used, risk rating, approvals, control owners, incidents and review dates. This should also include clarity on how risks, owners and mitigations or treatments are logged. The AI Risk Management toolkit has more information.

Organisational, managerial and practitioner responsibilities are clear, including who accepts residual risk.

2. Risk-based approval and assurance

Each use case is risk assessed in line with a risk appetite statement including a impact or likelihood score before procurement, pilot, deployment or material change.

Approval evidence covers intended benefit, non-AI alternatives, lawfulness, safeguarding, equality, ethics, privacy, security, accessibility, human oversight and business continuity.

Data protection, equality impact assessments, PSED (Public Sector Equality Duty) and Human Rights checks are completed where required and linked to the approval record.

Conditions of approval, acceptance thresholds, residual risks, review dates and stop or withdrawal criteria are documented.

Material changes to models, prompts, data, integrations, suppliers, terms or purpose trigger reassessment and reapproval.

3. Supplier and contract oversight

Due diligence tests supplier claims on functionality, limitations, accuracy, bias, security, data use and regulatory compliance.

Contracts cover data access, location, retention, deletion, reuse, model training, subcontractors, incidents, auditing, performance reporting and exit.

Suppliers must notify the organisation of material model, service, security or contractual changes.

Named contract owners monitor service levels, risks, incidents, updates, assurance evidence and corrective actions.

4. Operational oversight and human control

Approved workflows identify where human review, professional judgement and sign-off are mandatory.

Outputs entering records or informing practice are appropriately reviewed by the practitioner.

Managers use supervision and quality assurance to identify over-reliance, boundary breaches or inappropriate use.

Access controls, usage controls and technical restrictions support policy compliance.

Staff have clear routes for advice, challenge, incident reporting and protected escalation.

5. Audit and compliance assurance

An audit plan defines scope, frequency, sampling method, evidence requirements, responsible assurance function and reporting route.

Audits test whether only approved tools and uses are operating, required human review occurred, data rules were followed and records are accurate and complete.

Audit sampling is proportionate to risk and includes case records, outputs, user activity, exceptions, complaints and decisions influenced by AI.

Findings are reported to the governance forum and senior owner, with severity ratings, named actions, deadlines and follow-up verification.

Repeated, systemic or high-severity findings trigger escalation, increased sampling, control changes, suspension or withdrawal.

Independent assurance is considered for higher risk uses or where internal assurance is insufficient.

6. Monitoring, incidents and change control

The governance forum receives a regular oversight report covering usage, accuracy, corrections, bias, unequal impact, accessibility, security, incidents, complaints, benefits and control compliance.

Performance is reviewed across relevant groups, teams and settings to identify drift, exclusion or unequal outcomes.

Thresholds define when issues require investigation, corrective action, escalation, suspension or supplier remediation.

Incidents and near misses are logged, assessed, contained, investigated and reported through existing safeguarding, data, security and corporate risk routes.

Model drift, updates and changes in law, policy, practice or local context trigger reassessment.

Each tool has a scheduled review and explicit continuation, modification, suspension and withdrawal decisions.

7. Feedback, transparency and learning

Practitioners, managers, service users, and partner organisations have accessible routes to provide feedback, challenge use or raise concerns.

Organisations should consider how children, parents, carers and individuals who draw on care can inform the design and implementation of AI tools where they may affect people drawing on care and support.

Feedback, complaints, incidents, audit findings and evidence of benefit are logged, categorised, assigned and reviewed together by the governance forum.

Governance records show what was heard, the decision taken, action owner, timescale and, where no action is taken, the rationale.

Recording the tool on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standards (ATRS) has been considered – where relevant, this is best practice.

Learning informs approval conditions, controls, tools, contracts, policy, training, audit plans and monitoring thresholds.

Limitations and accountability are communicated transparently and a safe non-AI route is available where appropriate.

Quick assurance test for senior leaders

Before approval or continued use, senior leaders should be able to answer yes to the following:

Is there clear ownership, decision authority and documented risk acceptance?

Is the level of oversight and assurance proportionate to potential impact?

Are human control, auditability and accountability built into the workflow?

Do audit and monitoring provide reliable evidence of compliance, safety, fairness and benefit?

Are findings, incidents and feedback acted on and tracked to closure?

Are supplier changes and performance subject to effective oversight?

Can the organisation pause or withdraw the tool quickly?

Annex C checklist: considering ethics, risks and challenges when using AI in social care

Purpose

This checklist is intended to support practitioners in considering the risks and challenges associated with AI in their use in practice. This may be used as a starting point for organisations to develop their own checklists.

Professional judgement, human oversight and over-reliance

Before using or accepting an AI output, practitioners should check that AI is supporting, not replacing their professional judgement. This helps mitigate risks around reduced critical thinking, over-reliance and automation bias where AI outputs may be given undue weight because the tool appears authoritative.

Have I formed my own professional view before looking at, or relying on, the AI output?

Have I reviewed, challenged and amended the output where needed?

Have I added my own analysis, reflections, observations, context and professional judgement?

Have I considered whether I am giving too much weight to the AI output because it appears confident or authoritative?

Would I be able to explain and justify the final content without referring to AI as the decision-maker?

Accountability and governance

Accepting AI outputs without challenge, testing or review can lead to errors in case notes, records and documentation and may result in practitioners not fully owning their decisions. Practitioners should remain accountable for their use of AI.

Am I clear that I remain accountable for any final record, assessment, plan, letter or decision?

Is my use of AI in line with my organisation’s AI policy or local guidance?

Have I recorded or evidenced my own reasoning where appropriate?

Would my manager or supervisor be able to understand how AI supported the work and how I checked it?

Can I justify my decisions?

Accuracy and hallucination

AI may produce incorrect, incomplete or plausible-sounding content, including misunderstandings of transcripts or context. Outputs should be verified against source information and amended before being saved or used.

Have I checked the AI output against the original source information?

Have I checked names, dates, facts, chronology, actions and key details?

Have I removed or corrected anything that the AI appears to have invented, overstated or misunderstood?

Have I checked whether the AI has inferred conclusions that are not supported by the evidence?

Have I considered whether the AI summary is too neat, certain or simplified?

Have I checked whether important uncertainty, disagreement, risk or context has been lost?

Have I considered the consequences if an error were entered into a record or used in later work?

If appropriate, have I asked the AI to identify uncertainty or distinguish between evidence and possible inference?

Bias, fairness and equity

AI systems may also reflect or amplify bias in training data, design choices or deployment context, creating risks of unfair treatment, distorted analysis or unequal impacts. Practitioners and managers should be alert to bias when reviewing AI outputs.

Have I checked whether the output could unfairly represent, stereotype or disadvantage a person or group?

Have I considered whether the language used is judgemental, stigmatising, victim-blaming or deficit-focused?

Have I checked whether the person’s voice, wishes, feelings and lived experience are accurately reflected?

Have I checked whether different characteristics or circumstances may have influenced the way the output has been framed?

If something seems unclear, biased or unfair, have I questioned and amended it?

Where concerns about bias arise, do I know how to raise them through local feedback or governance routes?

Transparency, explainability and trust

Where AI is used by practitioners who are not able to explain (at a high level) what tools are being used, how they work and how outputs will be used, it risks undermining trust between practitioner and those they support. Understanding the basics of how AI tools work, and their limitations, will help practitioners get the most out of the tools.

Can I explain what information the tool captures, and how outputs will be used?

Do I understand the limitations of the tool?

Have I followed local policy on transparency, consent, agreement or approval?

If someone objects to AI being used, do I know what alternative process should be followed?

Privacy, security and data protection

Only approved tools should be used and personal or case data should not be entered into publicly available AI tools.

Is this tool approved by my organisation for this task?

Am I clear what information can and cannot be entered into the tool?

Have I followed local data protection, information governance and safeguarding requirements?

This focuses on using AI tools in practice and the AI Risk Management Toolkit provides advice and guidance on how to support and test the privacy and security of AI tools.

Multi-disciplinary or multi-agency settings

Different organisations may have different policies on how and when AI can be used, which may create barriers or uncertainty in multi-disciplinary settings. Practitioners should ensure that they are able to use AI in multi-agency settings before doing so.

Are other organisations involved in this meeting, assessment, record or plan?

Have I checked whether partner organisations have different policies on AI use?

Has AI use been agreed before the meeting or activity takes place?

Have participants been told what the AI tool will do and how outputs will be used?

Is there a clear alternative if AI use is not agreed?

Quick final check before saving, sharing or using AI-assisted work

Use this as a final ‘pause point’ before adding AI-assisted material to a record, plan, report, email or document.

I have checked the output against the original information.

I have corrected inaccuracies, omissions and unsupported conclusions.

I have checked for bias, unfairness, inappropriate language and loss of the person’s voice.

I have added my own professional judgement, reflections, context and observations.

I have complied with organisational policy, data protection requirements and safeguarding duties.

I have not used AI to make a decision about risk, need, eligibility, safeguarding, care planning or intervention.

I am satisfied that I can explain and stand behind the final version as my professional work.

Annex D: an introductory guide to AI for social care practitioners

This annex provides a short, practical introduction to AI for social care practitioners. It explains how AI works, how it may support practice, and the safeguards practitioners should apply when using it.

What AI is and how it works

Across government, the definition of AI adopted by OECD countries is used:

“An AI system is a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. Different AI systems vary in their levels of autonomy and adaptiveness after deployment”

AI systems use patterns in data to generate outputs such as text, summaries, predictions or recommendations. AI tools do not ‘think’; they predict outputs and responses based on the patterns and trends in data that the models are trained on. Some AI systems are able to act autonomously and interact with other AI systems to complete specific tasks.

In social care, common examples include transcription tools, summarisation tools, search tools and GenAI tools that produce text from a prompt.

AI tools are ‘trained’ on large datasets. Depending on the tool, these may include documents, webpages, numerical data and images. The AI is taught to learn and identify patterns to then make predictions and generate outputs based on these patterns. This is why AI tools are prone to bias and hallucinations.

GenAI works from a prompt: the instruction, question or information provided by a user. The tool looks for patterns in the information it has been trained on, and any information provided by the user (such as transcripts or documents), then generates a likely response. This response can appear fluent and human-like, but it does not understand.

AI use often involves:

input: a prompt or information, for example audio recordings or transcripts, text or documents, images or datasets

processing: the AI identifies patterns and predicts a likely response – like autocorrect on your phone, it predicts only the next most-likely word in a sequence and repeats this to create a full output

output: the user receives a draft, summary or answer to check and improve

AI does not:

think, have feelings or understand people, emotions, relationships or lived experiences

understand the full context of an event or person’s life or circumstances

It may help organise information, but practitioners should add professional judgement, context, observations, the person’s voice and understanding that effective social work requires.

AI systems can reflect biases that exist in the data used to train them. Practitioners should:

consider whether outputs could disadvantage, stereotype or unfairly represent individuals or groups

apply professional judgement to identify and address potential bias

Public AI tools should not be used for casework or personal information. Practitioners should only use tools approved by their organisation for the specific purpose and should follow local rules relating to:

information governance

data protection

consent

transparency and record-keeping

statutory and regulatory frameworks

How AI can support social care

AI should support practice, not replace practitioners’ judgements. Its main value is likely to be in:

reducing administrative burden

improving drafts and records

helping practitioners find or summarise information

supporting reflection

Using AI in social care: a quick guide for practitioners has more information.

Ensuring safety in AI use in social care

Safe AI use depends on keeping people in control. Practitioners do not need to be technical experts, but they should know:

what the tool is for

what information can be entered

how the output will be checked

where accountability sits

Ultimately, responsibility and accountability sit with the practitioner for all decisions they make.

The professional standards that apply to social work and social care practice, statutory frameworks and local policies and guidance continue to apply, irrespective of whether AI is used or not.

AI cannot replace professional judgements and the critical thinking that is fundamental to social care as a human-centred profession.

Practitioners should be transparent about their use of AI in line with organisational policy and local guidance.

Practitioners should avoid becoming over-reliant on AI and should continue to develop and use their own assessment, analysis, writing and decision-making skills.

The guidance using AI in social care: a quick guide for practitioners has more information on what to do before you use AI and what you should do after using it.
